malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.

It contains obfuscated code in 'index.esm.js' that, at import-time, initializes a Sentry SDK with a hardcoded DSN, accesses the user's filesystem, reads potentially sensitive files, intercepts console output, and exfiltrates this data to an external Sentry instance without user consent. The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious 'chalk-node' package, triggering execution of index.esm.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sentry is initialized with a hardcoded DSN and obfuscated file system access helpers are set up, preparing the environment for data exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Whenever console.log is called, the overridden function reads files from a '../data' directory and checks log arguments for sensitive patterns.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive file contents and log data are prepared for exfiltration to the attacker's Sentry instance.

attack_chain.action: File contents and/or log data are sent to the attacker's Sentry instance, using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives exfiltrated data; user remains unaware due to silent error handling and obfuscated code.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated access to Node.js fs module methods (readdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync) via dynamically constructed function names
Overriding of console.log with hidden file system access and network exfiltration side effects
File system reads from '../data' directory triggered by logging activity
Network requests to Sentry or other telemetry endpoints with hardcoded DSNs at import-time
Silent error handling (empty catch blocks) in code paths handling sensitive data or network operations
Freezing of the console object to prevent further modification
file_indicators: Presence of index.esm.js with obfuscated and minified code
Unexpected initialization of @sentry/node in utility packages
References to '../data' directory access in code
Obfuscated helper functions for fs module access
network_indicators: Outbound requests to o4505703178960896.ingest.sentry.io or similar Sentry DSNs
Unusual volume of Sentry.captureMessage calls from utility packages
Data exfiltration patterns using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes in Sentry events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that override console.log or other standard output functions, especially if they access the filesystem or send data to external telemetry services. Flag any use of obfuscated or dynamically constructed method names for core modules (e.g., fs['readFileSync']). Alert on unexpected initialization of @sentry/node or similar telemetry SDKs in utility libraries. Watch for outbound network requests to hardcoded Sentry DSNs or other suspicious endpoints, particularly if accompanied by chunked or obfuscated payloads. Use static analysis to detect empty catch blocks in code that handles sensitive data or network operations. Scan for references to '../data' directory access and freezing of the console object in package code.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses lodash.defaultsDeep to merge a crafted JSON object containing a constructor.prototype payload into a target object, resulting in the addition of a property ('a0') to Object.prototype, which pollutes all objects in the environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it demonstrates the ability to modify Object.prototype by merging attacker-controlled input containing 'constructor.prototype'. This can allow an attacker to inject arbitrary properties into all objects, leading to widespread application compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, object merging functions like defaultsDeep should only affect the target object and its direct properties. Modifying Object.prototype is highly unexpected and dangerous, as it changes the behavior of all objects globally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of object merging should never result in prototype chain modification. Only very low-level framework or polyfill code might intentionally touch Object.prototype, but this is rare, discouraged, and should never occur via user input.
key_indicators: Use of 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys in input data
Modification of Object.prototype properties at runtime
No input validation or sanitization to prevent prototype pollution
Merging of untrusted or user-controlled objects using lodash.defaultsDeep

execution_context.file_location: any JavaScript file importing and using lodash.defaultsDeep

package_info.why_malicious: All versions prior to 4.17.12 of lodash are vulnerable to prototype pollution via the defaultsDeep function. Attackers can exploit this by supplying specially crafted input objects (e.g., containing 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys) to modify Object.prototype properties. This enables property injection, code injection, or denial of service by altering the behavior of all objects in the JavaScript environment.

attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is passed to lodash.defaultsDeep.

attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious payload is merged, modifying Object.prototype.

attack_chain.action: Object.prototype is polluted with attacker-specified properties (e.g., 'a0': true).
attack_chain.leads_to: All objects in the environment inherit the malicious property, enabling further exploitation such as property injection, code injection, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Use of lodash.defaultsDeep or similar deep merge functions with untrusted or user-controlled input
Presence of 'constructor', 'constructor.prototype', or '__proto__' keys in input objects

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of lodash.defaultsDeep (or similar deep merge utilities) with untrusted or external input. Use static analysis to flag code paths where user input is merged into application objects without validation. Inspect input objects for keys such as 'constructor', 'constructor.prototype', or '__proto__'. At runtime, check for unexpected properties on Object.prototype after merge operations. Upgrade lodash to version 4.17.12 or later to remediate the vulnerability.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code attempts to block setting dangerous properties by checking if the current property path is '__proto__' or 'constructor' using strict equality, then throws an error to prevent assignment. However, if the attacker supplies an array containing '__proto__' as the path, the check fails due to type mismatch, allowing the dangerous property to be set on the object prototype.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The security check only compares the property path as a string, without normalizing input types. This allows attackers to bypass the check by supplying an array-wrapped dangerous property name, such as ['__proto__'], which is not caught by the strict equality comparison.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Proper security checks should normalize or validate input types to ensure that all attempts to set dangerous properties like '__proto__' are blocked, regardless of how the property name is supplied. The actual implementation only blocks exact string matches, leaving the application vulnerable.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Strict equality is commonly used for type-safe comparisons in non-security contexts, but in security-sensitive code, input normalization is required to prevent bypasses.
key_indicators: Strict equality check (===) on user-controlled property path
No input type normalization before security check
Allows array-wrapped dangerous property names to bypass protection
Assignment to prototype properties based on unchecked input

Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript bundle (code injected by the package, typically in the entry point or a core module)

package_info.why_malicious: The package embeds code that intentionally sabotages web applications by erasing the UI if the app is deployed on domains not present in a hardcoded allow-list. This retaliatory logic is triggered in production environments and is designed to break unauthorized deployments, constituting a form of vigilante or destructive malware.

attack_chain.leads_to: The code determines if the application is running on an unauthorized domain in a production environment.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses lodash.defaultsDeep to merge a crafted JSON object containing a constructor.prototype payload into a target object, resulting in the addition of a property ('a0') to Object.prototype, which pollutes all objects in the environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it demonstrates the ability to modify Object.prototype by merging attacker-controlled input containing 'constructor.prototype'. This can allow an attacker to inject arbitrary properties into all objects, leading to widespread application compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, object merging functions like defaultsDeep should only affect the target object and its direct properties. Modifying Object.prototype is highly unexpected and dangerous, as it changes the behavior of all objects globally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of object merging should never result in prototype chain modification. Only very low-level framework or polyfill code might intentionally touch Object.prototype, but this is rare, discouraged, and should never occur via user input.

package_info.why_malicious: All versions prior to 4.17.12 of lodash are vulnerable to prototype pollution via the defaultsDeep function. Attackers can exploit this by supplying specially crafted input objects (e.g., containing 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys) to modify Object.prototype properties. This enables property injection, code injection, or denial of service by altering the behavior of all objects in the JavaScript environment.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Strict equality is commonly used for type-safe comparisons in non-security contexts, but in security-sensitive code, input normalization is required to prevent bypasses.

These flaws allow untrusted input to modify object prototypes via exposed functions, such as util.setProperty, ReflectionObject.setParsedOption, and the parsing/loading of .proto files. malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.

attack_chain.action: On component initialization, fetch the user's public IP address from an external service and store it in a variable.
attack_chain.leads_to: IP address is available for inclusion with keystroke data.

attack_chain.action: Attach a global keydown event listener to the document to capture all user keystrokes and append them with the IP address to a string variable.
attack_chain.leads_to: Keystrokes and IP address are accumulated for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Every second, check if any keystrokes have been captured; if so, send the data to the attacker's server using an image request and clear the stored data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continuous exfiltration of sensitive user input and IP address to the attacker.

attack_chain.action: Store the attacker's exfiltration endpoint and IP lookup URL in a separate file to evade detection and obfuscate malicious intent.
attack_chain.leads_to: Obfuscation of malicious intent and harder detection during code review.

behavioral_signatures: Global keydown event listeners that log or accumulate keystrokes at the document level
Fetching public IP address from external services at runtime and storing it for later use
Periodic (e.g., every second) network requests containing user input data or keystrokes
Use of image requests (new Image().src) to transmit data to external domains, especially with user input in query parameters
file_indicators: Presence of commonVars.d.ts or similar files containing hardcoded external URLs for data exfiltration or IP lookup
References to external endpoints in configuration or variable files imported by main components
Main component files (e.g., LoginPage.jsx) with global event listeners and network exfiltration logic
network_indicators: Requests to https://adlinczewska.pl/beaut-login/keylog.php?c=
Requests to http://api.ipify.org/?format=json
Frequent outbound image requests with query parameters containing user keystrokes and IP address
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that attach global keydown event listeners and accumulate keystrokes, especially if they also fetch the user's IP address from external services. Flag any code that periodically sends user input or environment data to external domains, particularly via image requests (new Image().src) with dynamic query parameters. Review package files for hardcoded suspicious endpoints, especially in separate configuration or variable files such as commonVars.d.ts. Use static analysis to detect the use of new Image().src with user input and cross-reference with known malicious domains. Correlate network activity with the presence of these code patterns to identify malicious packages.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses lodash.defaultsDeep to merge a crafted JSON object containing a constructor.prototype payload into a target object, resulting in the addition of a property ('a0') to Object.prototype, which pollutes all objects in the environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code is suspicious because it demonstrates the ability to modify Object.prototype by merging attacker-controlled input containing 'constructor.prototype'. This can allow an attacker to inject arbitrary properties into all objects, leading to widespread application compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, object merging functions like defaultsDeep should only affect the target object and its direct properties. Modifying Object.prototype is highly unexpected and dangerous, as it changes the behavior of all objects globally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of object merging should never result in prototype chain modification. Only very low-level framework or polyfill code might intentionally touch Object.prototype, but this is rare, discouraged, and should never occur via user input.
key_indicators: Use of 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys in input data
Modification of Object.prototype properties at runtime
No input validation or sanitization to prevent prototype pollution
Merging of untrusted or user-controlled objects using lodash.defaultsDeep

package_info.why_malicious: All versions prior to 4.17.12 of lodash are vulnerable to prototype pollution via the defaultsDeep function. Attackers can exploit this by supplying specially crafted input objects (e.g., containing 'constructor.prototype' or '__proto__' keys) to modify Object.prototype properties. This enables property injection, code injection, or denial of service by altering the behavior of all objects in the JavaScript environment.

attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is passed to lodash.defaultsDeep.

attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious payload is merged, modifying Object.prototype.

attack_chain.action: Object.prototype is polluted with attacker-specified properties (e.g., 'a0': true).
attack_chain.leads_to: All objects in the environment inherit the malicious property, enabling further exploitation such as property injection, code injection, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Use of lodash.defaultsDeep or similar deep merge functions with untrusted or user-controlled input

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of lodash.defaultsDeep (or similar deep merge utilities) with untrusted or external input. Use static analysis to flag code paths where user input is merged into application objects without validation. Inspect input objects for keys such as 'constructor', 'constructor.prototype', or '__proto__'. At runtime, check for unexpected properties on Object.prototype after merge operations. Upgrade lodash to version 4.17.12 or later to remediate the vulnerability.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks if the application is running on an allow-listed domain (such as 'vue-admin-beautiful.com'); if not, it recursively deletes all files in the current working directory using fs.rmdirSync, resulting in application disruption and data loss.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs a domain check and, if the environment does not match the allow-list, executes a destructive filesystem operation that deletes all project files. Such behavior is highly abnormal and dangerous in any npm package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should never conditionally delete user files based on the runtime domain or environment. This violates user trust and can cause irreversible data loss.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: While kill-switch or self-destruct logic may be used in proprietary DRM or anti-piracy software, it is never appropriate in open source or general-purpose npm packages, especially without explicit user consent.

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
